name: Vera Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Short version: numbers, then more numbers. I'm the head buyer at Kestrel Auto Parts, which supplies brake pads, filters, batteries and the like to about 400 garages. I'm in at eight, look at what sold overnight, and spend the first hour with my forecasting setup. I built most of it with an AI assistant that I use all day. Then I haggle with the big parts makers, which is a game I enjoy. What wears me out is the shift to electric cars. Every year the old-engine parts sell a little less and I have to guess how fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say sensible, it's a good tool and not magic. At work I'd say keep using it where it works, and stop buying the dream. To friends I'd say it's a decent calculator, no more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my setup keeps its edge, and nobody's rushing past me. My job's secure. The thing keeping me up is something else: the shift to electric cars, which shrinks my catalogue of parts every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep refining my forecasting setup and use the time to work out the electric-car curve properly. I'd put a bit more into the pension, and look at whether Kestrel should carry more battery and charging parts. I'd also test a couple of other tools for supplier price checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Not thrilled, since I'm carrying the parts-shift worry, but not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the electric car shift is already pressing on you. How does that sit in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A plateau is good for me because everyone else has stopped trying new things and I haven't. A small advantage, compounded, is a lot, so I'd just keep getting a bit better each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use a plateau to your advantage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I forecast with old-engine models and I'm wrong by ten percent on brake pads, but by thirty on batteries. That's where the risk is. I'd use my spare hours on getting that right, because a wrong battery order ties up a lot of money.

say: It's a good tool and not **magic**, so keep using it where it works.
think: My setup keeps its **edge**, and my job is secure.
The thing keeping me up is the **electric car** shift, which shrinks my catalogue every year.
do: Refine my **forecasting** setup and study the electric-car curve properly.
Add to my **pension** and test a couple of tools for supplier price checks.
feel: **Okay**, not thrilled, because the parts-shift worry stays.
S0.quote: A small advantage, compounded, is a lot, so I'd just keep getting a bit better each month.
fieldNote: Vera's **adaptive** habit is to use a plateau to keep improving, not to relax.
Her real pressure is the **electric car** shift, which is independent of AI.

steps.text: Refine my forecasting setup for battery and charging parts
Test two other tools for supplier price checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say good, we should get on with it and decide who does what. To friends I'd say it's real and it'll affect your job whatever you do. Online I'd stay out, because people are tribal about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, about half my day is things software does well: forecasting, comparing quotes, drafting orders. I already do most of that with assistants. What's left is negotiating, spotting trouble in a supplier, and deciding how much risk to take. But I won't pretend that isn't thinner than it was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build faster. I'd move more of Kestrel's reordering to automated agents with my checks on top, and I'd ask for the team to be put into that. I'd also move my own role towards supplier strategy and the electric transition. And I'd start putting aside a little more, because it can't hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested and a bit watchful. I'm good with change, but even I get nervous when the ground moves under a whole team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your own job is something software would do well within a few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The junior buyers doing reorders and quote comparison are most exposed, about four of our eleven buyers. The people who keep relationships with the big makers aren't, at least for a while. The dividing line is who can do the thing that isn't on the spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Kestrel is at risk, and who isn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half. Maybe a bit more by the end of the period. I'd rather measure it than guess, so I'd track my own hours.

say: We should **get on with it** and decide who does what.
It's real, and it'll affect your job **whatever** you do.
think: About **half** my day is things software does well, and I already do most of it with assistants.
What's left is **negotiating** and spotting trouble, but it's thinner than before.
do: Move Kestrel's reordering to **automated** agents with my checks on top.
Shift my role to **supplier strategy** and the electric transition, and save a little more.
feel: **Interested** and watchful, since even I get nervous when the ground moves.
S1.quote: The dividing line is who can do the thing that isn't on the spreadsheet.
fieldNote: Vera sees her day as about **half** exposed, and she'd rather measure than guess.
She expects about four of eleven buyers to be **at risk**, a concrete and unsentimental view.

steps.text: Move Kestrel's reordering to automated agents with my checks
Shift my role to supplier strategy and electric parts
Track my own hours to see what software does
Add a little more to savings each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a proper plan, fast, and I'd offer to draft one. To friends I'd say it's the real thing and sensible people should adjust. Online I'd say we need both sides, government and business, to help people through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the one that gets me. The tools I use every day will be doing my job on their own in two years, and the edge of knowing them goes. I'd be quietly scared. I'd still be better placed than most, but that's cold comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd work out what we'd need to live on and for how long. I'd pull everything non-essential. Then I'd write a plan for Kestrel's board showing how to move to an automated buying setup, with me running it and a short list of roles that stay. If it came to it, I'd offer myself as the person who audits it. I'd also check our investments, and talk to a financial adviser, once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A lot of it is the speed, but I'm also curious. It's a bit like riding a fast horse: you don't get off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Jonas runs a bike repair shop with his brother. Does that change how you see two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas works with bikes and tools, so the hands-on side lasts about three years after the desk work. That's our cushion. His shop's also vulnerable to people having less money, so it's not safe at all. But it gives us a second source of income that isn't tied to AGI directly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write the plan, and I'd put a figure on it. If I show the board the savings, they'd rather have me run the automated buying than hire consultants. That's my bet, and it might not work, but it's my best shot.

say: We need a proper **plan**, fast, and I'll offer to draft one.
Government and **business** both have to help people through.
think: The tools I use daily will do my job on their own, and my **edge** goes.
I'd be better placed than most, but that's **cold comfort**.
do: Work out what we'd need to **live on** and for how long, and pull non-essentials.
Write a plan for **Kestrel's board** showing how I'd run an automated buying setup.
feel: **Anxious**, curious too, like riding a fast horse.
S2.quote: If I show the board the savings, they'd rather have me run the automated buying than hire consultants.
fieldNote: Vera's **bet** is that she can run the automated setup, which uses her adaptive strengths.
Jonas's **bike shop** is a second income that lasts longer but is not safe.

steps.text: Work out how long the household can live on savings
Write a plan for the board to automate buying
Offer to be the person who audits the setup
Meet a financial adviser once to check our investments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is long enough to do this well, so let's plan it. To friends I'd say learn the tools and keep your savings up. Online I'd say retraining and a safety net, funded by those who benefit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is a runway and I'd use it. It's still alarming that it all ends in 2031, but I know I'm able to move. I'd say I'm uneasy, not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the systems underneath: machine learning basics, data pipelines, enough to be a person who builds the buying tools, not only uses them. I'd keep building my own tools and get Kestrel to adopt them. I'd start a small consulting side-line, helping smaller distributors set up buying automation, and I'd invest steadily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a lot of energy. More like a project than a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do five years change the plan you'd write?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be writing a rescue plan. With five I could build a business case, then a pilot, then a roll-out, and maybe a company of my own. I'd have time to make it solid, and to get Jonas's shop on a firmer footing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay at Kestrel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, for a while. I like the firm and the people. But if the board wanted to cut buyers, I'd prefer to leave early with a plan than be pushed late. I'd think about a move to a bigger distributor that's ahead on this.

say: Five years is long enough to do this **well**, so let's plan it.
Retraining and a safety net should be funded by those who **benefit**.
think: Five years is a **runway**, and I know I'm able to move.
I'm **uneasy**, not scared, because I can act.
do: Learn **machine learning** basics and data pipelines to build buying tools.
Start a small **consulting** side-line for smaller distributors and invest steadily.
feel: **Uneasy** with lots of energy, more like a project than a threat.
S3.quote: I'd prefer to leave early with a plan than be pushed late.
fieldNote: Vera's adaptive instinct turns five years into a **business case**, pilot and roll-out.
She'd rather leave **early** with a plan than be pushed late, which says something about her risk comfort.

steps.text: Learn machine learning basics and data pipelines
Start consulting for smaller distributors on buying automation
Invest a fixed amount each month
Look at bigger distributors that are ahead on automation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say a decade is generous, so use it. To friends I'd say don't get complacent, because it'll be sooner than it looks. Online I'd say share the gains and fund the retraining early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's an opportunity as much as a risk. I'll be 53, with a lot of skill and a strong cushion. If I use the time well, I could be running something by then. I'm calm, though I wouldn't call it relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep pushing at Kestrel, moving into strategy. I'd build a small side business in purchasing tools and invest every month. I'd also help Mila and Oskar pick things that build judgement and people skills, and check where the electric-car shift takes the whole motor trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. I'm optimistic, actually, and I'd say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you build or start with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them that the world will change fast and that curiosity is worth more than any single skill. I'd show them what I do. Mila's old enough to see what a tool can and can't do, and I'd rather my daughter sees a tool first-hand than hears fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you talk to Mila and Oskar about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a small firm that sells smart buying systems to garages and parts shops, with a couple of people. Not a startup dream, more a sensible business. If it fails, I'm still employable.

say: A decade is generous, so **use it**.
Share the **gains** and fund the retraining early, before people are pushed out.
think: It's an **opportunity** as much as a risk, and I'm calm but not relaxed.
With strong savings and skill, I could be **running something** by 53.
do: Move into **strategy** at Kestrel and build a small side business in purchasing tools.
Show Mila and Oskar what the tools can and **can't** do.
S4.quote: Curiosity is worth more than any single skill.
fieldNote: Vera is **calm** because she has time, a cushion and skills that adapt.
Her ideal is a **small firm** selling buying systems to garages, not a startup dream.

steps.text: Move into purchasing strategy at Kestrel
Build a small buying-tools business on the side
Invest a set amount every month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the tools I use every day would do my job on their own and my edge would vanish before I'd had time to move. What would help is a real warning period, support for a business start-up or retraining, and a safety net that isn't a lottery. If governments and firms agreed on that, I'd feel much better.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Being good with the tools doesn't make me safe. People think the adaptable ones are fine, and we aren't. We adaptable ones just move faster.

headlineQuote: Being good with the tools doesn't make me safe.
portrait: Vera is a 43-year-old head **auto parts buyer** at Kestrel, with a bike-shop partner, two children and a mortgage.
She is centrist and **adaptive**: she built her own forecasting setup and uses AI all day.
She is uneasy about the **electric car** shift even before AI, and anxious when AGI is two years away.
Her answer to every scenario is to **build**: automation plans, a consulting side-line and savings.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario, because the tools she uses would do her job before she could move.
whatWouldHelp: A real **warning period**, support for retraining or a start-up, and a safety net that isn't a lottery.
